mechanism: Video2X is an open-source pipeline that splits a video into frames with ffmpeg, runs each frame through a super-resolution network (Real-ESRGAN, Real-CUGAN or Anime4K shaders) on a Vulkan-capable GPU, then re-encodes the frames with the original audio. Quality depends on the model chosen and on the GPU; speed is frames per second of the network, which is slow on CPU. Interpolation (RIFE) can be run in the same pass.
claim: A free local tool upscales video to higher resolution with AI models, offered as an alternative to paid upscalers.
why_not_testable: Needs a Vulkan GPU build for macOS and a paid Topaz-on-fal comparison, and the Intel Mac has no useful GPU for it.
needs: Apple silicon or a Vulkan GPU, and a fal account for the Topaz comparison
one_line: Video2X chops video into frames, upscales each with a neural net on the GPU and restitches it; free, but the quality gap to Topaz is unmeasured.
idea_why: Frame-wise super-resolution is a well-established technique and a free route to a final-pass upscale.
breakdown: Install Video2X (release binary or build) on the M5, feed it a generated 720p clip, choose a Real-ESRGAN model and a 2x factor. Run the same clip through Topaz on fal and compare by eye plus a simple metric such as sharpness variance or a no-reference score. Record seconds per clip and any flicker between frames, since frame-wise methods can shimmer. A person would judge faces and text, which metrics miss.

mechanism: Video templates are Remotion (React/TypeScript) projects with declared photo slots, copy fields and settings. A Python CLI (vvv.py) exposes describe and validate commands so an agent fills inputs first and edits source only if needed, then renders and runs checks. The reference-video mode measures a supplied file (beats, shot lengths, still frames) and rebuilds it on the closest template.

mechanism: Track Then Bind runs a promptable video tracker over every candidate object and labels each with a track number. A frozen vision-language model answers a static question at a moment when the identifying evidence is visible, binding the target to a track. The final answer is computed from the tracked state in text, not by asking the model to re-watch the video.
claim: Reaches 55.4% on the hardest Perception Test cup games against 41.5% for the best published model, with no training.
why_not_testable: Needs a video tracker plus a 32B vision-language model, and there is no local LLM on this Mac.
needs: A GPU and a vision-language model
one_line: Models lose track of which cup hides the ball; binding identity once, then letting a tracker carry it, lifts accuracy without training.
idea_why: The split between identity binding and tracking is plausible and the gains are large, but only the authors have measured it.
breakdown: Fetch the paper's code if released, run the tracker (a SAM-style video model) on a few public shell-game clips, and ask a hosted VLM one static question per bound track. Score against the Perception Test cup-game answers. The tracker needs a GPU, so this is a rented-machine job.

mechanism: A feature-based controller picks, per task, whether a coding agent uses primitive tool calls, a macro skill, or a macro with fallback. A finite-state executor catches macro failure and drops to micro steps to recover. Evaluation uses a deterministic coding protocol with verifier-defined success and cost.

mechanism: Motion transfer takes a still image of a character and a reference video of a person moving, estimates the pose sequence from the video, and generates the character performing that motion. Viggle is a hosted service; comparable open routes are Wan 2.2 Animate and Kling Motion Control. Output consistency depends on pose estimation and the model's handling of the character's identity.
claim: A free tool makes a still character copy the movement of a reference video.
why_not_testable: Hosted service needing an account, and the open alternatives need a GPU.
needs: A Viggle or Kling account, or a GPU for Wan 2.2 Animate
one_line: Motion transfer reads poses from a reference clip and drives a still character with them; free tier versus Kling and Wan is untested.
idea_why: The technique works in general; whether the free tier is good enough for an AI influencer track is unmeasured.
breakdown: Pick one synthetic character still and one licensed or self-filmed reference move. Run it through Viggle, Kling Motion Control and Wan 2.2 Animate, then score identity drift, hand artefacts and cost per five seconds. Use only synthetic characters, never a real person's likeness. mechanism: A Claude Code hook runs before each prompt is submitted and reads the session's token count and the time since the last request. If the prompt cache has probably expired (cache lifetime is short) and the context is large, it warns and suggests compacting first, and it can block sub-agent spawns when usage-window use is above a threshold. A commenter reports the same approach cut spawned agents from 365 to 27 over 75 days.
claim: A usage-guard mod protects the usage window; a commenter's version cut 365 agent spawns to 27.
verdict_question: Does the repo's hook flag a warning when fed a synthetic transcript with an expired cache gap and over 500k tokens, yes or no?
probe_title: agent-usage-guard: does its hook warn on a synthetic transcript with a stale cache and large context?
one_line: A prompt-time hook warns when the cache has gone cold and the context is huge, one user says it cut agent spawns from 365 to 27.
idea_why: Cold-cache, large-context resubmission is a real way to burn a usage window, and a pre-submit check is cheap.
breakdown: Clone the repo into the sandbox, read its hook, and build a small synthetic transcript with a timestamp gap and a large token count. Feed it to the hook and see whether it warns. Then compare its thresholds with our own runs' usage logs from bin/usage.py. Wiring it into Proteus would need a hook-file edit, which Luke's rules treat separately.
